hook: John Searle was born in Denver, Colorado, in 1932 and studied philosophy at the University of Wisconsin before winning a Rhodes Scholarship to Oxford, where he earned his doctorate under J. L. Austin and P. F. Strawson. He joined the philosophy department at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1959 and remained there for the rest of his career, becoming the Slusser Professor of Philosophy of Mind and Language. Building on his early work in speech act theory, he published Minds, Brains, and Programs in 1980, introducing the Chinese Room thought experiment: a person who manipulates Chinese symbols by following an English rulebook can produce correct answers without understanding a word of Chinese, which Searle argued shows that running the right program is not sufficient for genuine understanding. The argument became one of the most debated texts in philosophy of mind and cognitive science, directly challenging the claim that a sufficiently sophisticated computer program could think. He continued to develop the argument and its implications for consciousness across decades of subsequent books, including The Rediscovery of the Mind (1992), and remained an active commentator on AI and machine understanding into the era of large language models.

quick_facts: Born in Denver, Colorado, in 1932, and earned his D.Phil. at Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar under J. L. Austin
Joined the University of California, Berkeley philosophy department in 1959 and taught there until 2017
Published Speech Acts: An Essay in the Philosophy of Language in 1969
Introduced the Chinese Room thought experiment in Minds, Brains, and Programs (1980)
Held the Slusser Chair of Philosophy of Mind and Language at Berkeley

achievements.title: Speech Acts: An Essay in the Philosophy of Language (1969)
achievements.impact: Extended J. L. Austin's speech act theory into a systematic account of how utterances perform actions, a foundational text in philosophy of language.

achievements.title: Minds, Brains, and Programs (1980)
achievements.impact: Introduced the Chinese Room argument against the claim that symbol manipulation alone constitutes understanding, becoming one of the most cited and debated papers in cognitive science.

achievements.title: The distinction between strong and weak AI
achievements.impact: Coined the terms distinguishing the claim that an appropriately programmed computer literally has a mind from the claim that computers can only simulate mental processes, a distinction still used in debates over machine consciousness.

achievements.title: The Rediscovery of the Mind (1992)
achievements.impact: Argued against both dualism and computational functionalism, proposing that consciousness is a biological phenomenon caused by brain processes.
